title: Large anomalous shifts of potassium-39 Feshbach resonances
authors: Ali Zaheer, Mohammed Bouras, Krzysztof Giergiel, Rudolf Grimm, Andrei Sidorov, Peter Hannaford
abstract: We report the observation of large anomalous shifts, up to +7.5 G, of the positions of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms confined in a 1063.9 nm optical dipole trap (ODT) at temperatures up to around 35 μK and trap depths up to about 136 μK. When the atom cloud is cooled to lower temperatures, by reducing the trap depth of the ODT, the shifts decrease proportionally with trap depth and approach zero at zero depth. We show that the large observed shifts originate from a large differential ac Stark shift between the incoming pair of potassium-39 atoms and the weakly bound Feshbach molecule, which in turn originates from an unexpectedly large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule. The polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules extracted from the measured shifts of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G resonances are about four to seven times the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms, that is, about four to seven times larger than the usual polarizability of weakly bound Feshbach molecules. The large polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules are attributed to a near-coincidence between the frequency of the 1063.9 nm ODT laser and the frequency of a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the lowest triplet a3Σ+u potential to a vibrational level of the excited b3Σ+g potential. Other potassium-39 Feshbach resonances we have studied exhibit a zero or very small shift, corresponding to molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms.
summary: The researchers observed unusually large anomalous shifts in specific Feshbach resonances of potassium-39 atoms trapped by an optical dipole trap. They determined these shifts arise from a substantial differential ac Stark shift, pointing to molecular polarizabilities four to seven times larger than expected. This finding highlights the sensitivity of resonance spectroscopy to near-resonant laser coupling with underlying molecular transitions.
main_problem: The study reports observing large anomalous shifts of specific Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms confined within an optical dipole trap.
main_result: These large shifts are attributed to unexpectedly large dynamic polarizabilities of the weakly bound Feshbach molecules, which are significantly larger than previously expected for such systems.
method: The shift is measured by tracking the resonance position as a function of the optical trap depth and temperature, relating this shift to differential ac Stark effects.
model_or_system: The system involves ultracold potassium-39 atoms interacting via Feshbach resonances in an optical dipole trap (ODT). Theoretical models use coupled-channel scattering approaches involving singlet and triplet molecular potentials.
key_observables: Anomalous resonance shifts (up to +7.5 G), the dependence of these shifts on ODT depth, and the extracted dynamic polarizabilities ($\alpha_{mol}$).
important_parameters: Potassium-39 ($^{39}	ext{K}$), Feshbach resonances at 33.6 G and 39.9 G, trapping laser wavelength (1063.9 nm), temperatures up to $\sim 35 \mu	ext{K}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a spherically symmetric 3D-Gaussian trapping potential and uses thermal averaging over the trap depth.
figures_summary: Figures show calculated resonance positions, Zeeman energy level curves for molecular states, and plots detailing how the measured shift depends on the ODT trap depth and temperature.
paper_structure: The paper first reports the observation of large shifts, then analyzes the dependence on trapping parameters to isolate the source (differential ac Stark shift), and finally attributes this effect to a near-coincidence between the laser frequency and a molecular transition.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly sensitive probe into the dynamic polarizabilities of weakly bound molecules, revealing strong coupling mechanisms that deviate significantly from simple predictions based on atomic polarizabilities. This is crucial for high-precision quantum control using optical traps.
